title: Hereditary discrepancy and factorization norms (AimPL) — Problem 1.2: Beck-Fiala for random set systems

problems.sourceStatement: Each element $i\in [n]$ lies in $t$ randomly selected sets from $\mathcal{S}$. They show that when $m\ge n$, hereditary discrepancy of the set system is $O(\sqrt{t\log t})$ whp. When $n\ge m^t$, hereditary discrepancy is $O(1)$. An open question is to explore this setting for the remaining range of parameters i.e. when $n^{1/t} < m < n$.
problems.problem: Determine the hereditary discrepancy of random sparse set systems: with $n$ elements and $m$ sets, each element placed in $t$ uniformly random sets, what is the hereditary discrepancy with high probability, especially in the intermediate parameter regime $n^{1/t} < m < n$?
problems.wordDescription: This is a probabilistic version of the Beck-Fiala conjecture due to Esther Ezra and Shachar Lovett. In the model where each element is assigned to $t$ random sets, they proved: (i) when $m \geq n$ the hereditary discrepancy is $O(\sqrt{t\log t})$ with high probability, via a combination of the Lovász Local Lemma and partial matchings; and (ii) when $n \gg m^t$ the hereditary discrepancy is $O(1)$, via an analysis of the lattice spanned by sparse vectors. The interesting open case is the intermediate range $n^{1/t} < m < n$, where neither regime applies. Follow-up work by Hoberg and Rothvoss made progress: a Fourier-analytic argument gives discrepancy at most 1 when $n \geq \Theta(m^2 \log m)$, and a subsequent paper shows expected discrepancy $O(\sqrt{t})$ over the whole range when $t = \Omega((\log\log m)^2)$; an $\Omega(\sqrt{t})$ spectral lower bound (e.g. for $n = m = 2t$) shows this is tight.
problems.mathematicalConditions: Let $\mathcal{S} = (X, \Sigma)$ be a random set system with $|X| = n$ and $|\Sigma| = m$, where each element $x \in X$ is placed into $t$ sets chosen uniformly at random from $\Sigma$ (the $t$-tuple of sets containing $x$ is uniform among the $\binom{m}{t}$ possibilities). Determine the asymptotic behavior, with high probability, of $\mathrm{herdisc}(X, \Sigma)$, in particular in the regime $n^{1/t} < m < n$ not covered by the two known bounds ($m \geq n \Rightarrow O(\sqrt{t\log t})$; $n \gg m^t \Rightarrow O(1)$).

literature.title: E. Ezra, S. Lovett, On the Beck-Fiala conjecture for random set systems, APPROX/RANDOM 2016 (LIPIcs vol. 60, 29:1-29:10); Random Structures & Algorithms 54(4):665-675, 2019
literature.description: The source paper for this problem: proves $O(\sqrt{t\log t})$ when $|\Sigma| \geq |X|$ and $O(1)$ when $|X| \gg |\Sigma|^t$, and poses the intermediate regime as open.

literature.title: R. Hoberg, T. Rothvoss, A Fourier-analytic approach for the discrepancy of random set systems, arXiv:1806.04484, 2018
literature.description: Fourier-analytic method showing discrepancy at most 1 with high probability when $n \geq \Theta(m^2 \log m)$, improving the $O(1)$ regime of Ezra-Lovett (which required $n \gg m^t$).

literature.title: R. Hoberg, T. Rothvoss, On the discrepancy of random low degree set systems, arXiv:1810.03374, 2018
literature.description: Shows the expected discrepancy is $O(\sqrt{t})$ for the entire range of $n$ and $m$, provided $t = \Omega((\log\log m)^2)$; also notes the $\Omega(\sqrt{t})$ spectral lower bound (e.g. $n = m = 2t$) and that the problem is open even for simple hypergraphs (pairwise intersecting edges in at most one element).

problems.verificationNotes: Verified on 2026-08-25. The problem and its two bounds match Ezra-Lovett (arXiv:1511.00583; APPROX/RANDOM 2016; journal version RSA 54(4):665-675, 2019). Two minor clarifications relative to the AimPL text: the paper states the $O(1)$ regime as $|X| \gg |\Sigma|^t$ (strictly larger), and the intermediate range is $m \leq n \leq m^t$ (i.e. $n^{1/t} \leq m \leq n$). Follow-up progress by Hoberg-Rothvoss (arXiv:1806.04484, arXiv:1810.03374) is confirmed; the full conjecture for the intermediate regime remains open as of 2026.
problems.statusDetails: When $m\ge n$, hereditary discrepancy of the set system is $O(\sqrt{t\log t})$ whp. When $n\ge m^t$, hereditary discrepancy is $O(1)$. The remaining range $n^{1/t} < m < n$ is open (with subsequent partial progress by Hoberg and Rothvoss).
